comments.author: @chamindaabeykoon7617
comments.text:
Sri Lanka was not subjected to comprehensive territorial conquest by the Portuguese, Dutch, or British. Although these European powers employed sustained military force to establish and maintain dominion over the island’s littoral regions, their authority did not extend to the interior polities, most notably the Kingdom of Kandy, which preserved its sovereignty through diplomatic maneuvering, strategic geography, and periodic military resistance.

The transfer of sovereignty over the entire island to the British Crown occurred only in 1815, pursuant to the Kandyan Convention, a formal diplomatic instrument negotiated with the Kandyan aristocracy. This political transition was effected through legal and administrative mechanisms rather than through the culmination of a successful military campaign. As such, the unification of the island under British rule represents a constitutional and diplomatic act, rather than a conventional act of conquest.

comments.text: Correct me if I’m wrong, but Sri Lanka used to be called Ceylon. Why was it changed.

replies.author: @BestTravelDocumentary4k
replies.text: You are completely correct! The name was changed from Ceylon to 'Free, Sovereign and Independent Republic of Sri Lanka' in 1972 when it became a republic, shedding its colonial-era name to embrace its traditional native identity ('Sri Lanka' means 'resplendent island'). Do you enjoy learning about the history behind country name changes?"
